pass_a_gloss: Logos 5. [Lemma, Isaiah 50:5-8:] But I do not disobey, nor speak against. My back I have given to scourges, and my cheeks to blows, and my face I did not turn away from shame of spittings, and the Lord became my helper. Because of this I was not turned back, but I set my face like solid rock, and I knew that I will surely not be shamed, because the one who justified me draws near. Through the things already read before, or examined before, he has made a very great outcry against the disobedience of the Jews. For he said that, I came and there was no man, I called and there was not the one obeying, and having thrown in between the person of those who accepted the faith, and saying: The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction to know when it is needed to speak a word, and the things brought next to these, and [they] raising thanksgiving voices. The very person of Christ runs in again, being eager to set beside his own obedience the madnesses of the Jews, so that he might wholly convict them being hateful to God, and lifting a haughty and harsh neck to the one calling to salvation. For I have called, he says, and there was not the one obeying. They became sluggish toward obedience, slow and wholly without understanding toward the need to grasp what leads to benefit for them, and the things through which it was likely that they could escape, and very much without toil, both the tyranny of sin and the plots of the devilish perversity. But they disobeyed, and I do not disobey. For the God and Father having willed to sum up all things in me, both the things in the heaven and upon the earth, I let myself down toward emptying, and I came down into the measures of the human poverty, having appeared a man so that I might become obedient also until death, and death of a cross. I have given then my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows. And my face I did not turn away from shame of spittings. For these things happened to him to suffer, the boorishness of the Jews acting drunkenly outrageous toward him, and Pilate tearing him with scourges, and one of the unholy attendants insulting and striking him, and others spitting on him. But the one aim for the one suffering was to carry through to an end the good will of the Father. pass_b_english: “But I do not disobey, nor do I speak against it. I have given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting; and the Lord became my helper. Therefore I was not put to confusion, but I set my face like a solid rock, and I knew that I would never be put to shame; for He who justified me draws near” (Isaiah 50:5–8).

In the passages already read, or rather already examined, he has raised a very great outcry against the disobedience of the Jews. For he said: “I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was none to answer” (Isaiah 50:2). He then brought in between them the person of those who accepted the faith, saying: “The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, to know when I must speak a word” (Isaiah 50:4), with what follows these words, and they raised their voices in thanksgiving. Now the person of Christ Himself enters again, as He is eager to set His own obedience against the madness of the Jews, so as to expose them completely as hateful to God, since they lift a proud and harsh neck against Him who calls them to salvation.

“For I have called,” He says, “and there was none to answer.” They have grown sluggish toward obedience, slow and wholly without understanding when it came to grasping what would bring them profit, and the means by which they might well have escaped, and very easily, both the tyranny of sin and the plots of the devil’s malice. “But while they disobeyed, I do not disobey. For when God the Father willed to sum up all things in me, things in heaven and things on earth (Ephesians 1:10), I lowered myself to self-emptying and came down into the limits of human poverty, appearing as a man, that I might become obedient even to death, and death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8). So I have given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows; and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isaiah 50:6).

For these are the very things He came to suffer, when the boorishness of the Jews raged against Him like drunken men: Pilate tore Him with scourges (John 19:1), one of the unholy attendants insulted and struck Him (John 18:22), and others spat on Him (Matthew 26:67). But the One who suffered had a single aim: to carry the good will of the Father through to the end. choices.english: brought in between them the person of those who accepted the faith
choices.why: The genitive absolutes mark an interlude: the believers speak Isaiah 50:4 and give thanks, then Christ speaks again.

choices.english: to sum up all things in me
choices.why: Ephesians 1:10, put in Christ's own mouth.

choices.english: the boorishness of the Jews raged against Him like drunken men
choices.why: ἐμπαροινέω, to behave like a drunkard toward someone; Cyril's polemic is translated as written.
καταξαίνω, to tear like carded wool; the scourging of John 19:1.
The sufferer's one aim was the Father's good will.
